text: More than 14,000 years ago, the Natufians lived where Israel, Palestine, Jordan and Syria are today.
At the end of the last Ice Age, their land was woodland, full of wild food.
src: c. 12,500 BCE: A pita-like bread of wild cereal seeds and tubers is made / mostly Israel and the Palestinian territories, also Syria, Lebanon, Jordan

The Natufian culture grew up in the Levant at the end of the last Ice Age / The Levant was then woodland, not the dry, barren and thorny landscape of today, and it offered more than a hundred kinds of edible cereals, fruits, nuts and other plants

text: They hunted gazelles, deer and wild boar, and gathered wild grains, almonds, acorns and pistachios.
Without farming, some still lived in stone houses and were the first known to store food.
src: hunted mountain and goitered gazelles above all, as well as deer, aurochs, wild boar / They collected wild cereals, legumes, almonds, acorns and pistachios
The Natufians lived by hunting and gathering / round stone structures of Ain Mallaha / Natufian sites are the first to show evidence of food storage

text: They cut wild grain with stone sickles and made one of the oldest breads known.
At one place they may even have planted rye on purpose.
src: They cut wild cereals with stone sickles and made a bread-like food thousands of years before farming / A pita-like bread of wild cereal seeds and tubers is made, among the oldest known bread-like foods
Some evidence also suggests the deliberate cultivation of rye at Tell Abu Hureyra

text: The dead were buried with necklaces and bracelets of shell, bone and deer teeth.
In one village an old person was buried together with a puppy.
src: Grave goods were typically made of shell, red-deer teeth, bone and stone, and the dead were given pendants, bracelets, necklaces
At ʿAin Mallaha, about 12,000 BCE, an elderly person was buried with a puppy four to five months old

text: Their artists liked to carve animals most of all.
One small stone carving of a couple is now in the British Museum.
src: animals, which seem to have been the favourite subject of Natufian art
The Ain Sakhri lovers, a carved stone found in a cave in the Judean desert and now held at the British Museum

text: Their time ended about 11,500 years ago, and their descendants may have been the region’s first farmers.
Later peoples of the Levant were mainly descended from the Natufians.
src: c. 9,500 BCE: The Natufian period ends at the very beginning of the Holocene / they may be the ancestors of the region’s first farmers
Ancient DNA shows that later Levantines, from the Neolithic to the Bronze Age, descended mainly from the Natufians
